# Vignette: Adaeze

Adaeze is a 72-year-old widowed woman who has spent most of her adult life working in forestry in a rural region of West Africa. She knows the land the way other people know their own faces — the particular lean of certain trees after the rainy season, the sounds the canopy makes before a storm. For decades, the forest was her workplace and her sanctuary, a place where the logic of living things made sense to her.

That sense of order collapsed seven years ago when armed conflict swept through her region with almost no warning. Adaeze was in the field with two junior colleagues when fighters moved through the tree line. What followed was not a single explosion or a single moment of violence but hours of sustained terror — gunfire, the smell of smoke from burning structures in the nearby village, the sound of people screaming at a distance she could not measure. She and her colleagues hid beneath the dense undergrowth, pressing their bodies into the earth for what felt like an entire lifetime. One of her colleagues, a young man she had mentored for three years, was struck by a stray bullet while trying to shift position. Adaeze held his body against hers and kept her hand over his mouth, not because it would save him, but because she did not know what else to do. He died before the fighters moved on.

She walked out of the forest that evening carrying his identification card in her pocket. She has never spoken about what she did with her hand over his mouth. She believes she will never speak of it.

In the years since, Adaeze has continued working — or trying to. She returned to forestry because it was the only life she had ever built, but the forest is no longer what it was to her. When she walks beneath a heavy canopy now, her body does not relax the way it once did. Instead, something tightens in her chest, and she finds herself scanning the tree line in a way that has nothing to do with her professional assessment of the land. She startles violently at the crack of a fallen branch. On two occasions she has dropped to the ground without deciding to, her body acting before her mind could catch up.

She sleeps poorly. Most nights she wakes between two and four in the morning with her heart striking hard against her ribs, the images from that afternoon assembling themselves without her permission. She does not always remember the dream, but she always wakes knowing where she has been. During the day she finds her concentration fractured. She will stand at the edge of a survey plot holding her clipboard and realize she has read the same notation four times without absorbing it.

Since her husband died three years ago — from illness, not from the conflict — the loneliness has made everything heavier. She lives alone in a small house at the edge of the forest reserve where she works. Her adult children are in the city and call on weekends. She tells them she is fine. She has become skilled at being fine on the telephone.

What troubles her most, she says, is not the fear itself but what the fear has taken from her. She used to feel at home in the world in a way that required no effort. Now she feels like a stranger inside her own body, inside her own landscape. She describes herself as someone who is always waiting — though she cannot say precisely what she is waiting for. She moves through her days with a kind of careful vigilance, doing her work, eating her meals, watching the trees she has tended for decades, and carrying, very quietly, the weight of a young man's last breath against her palm.
